# 1 Enoch — Reader's Guide
**Guide:** HESED | **Category:** Pseudepigrapha (PS)

---

## At a Glance

| | |
|---|---|
| **Attribution** | Enoch, seventh from Adam (Gen 5:18–24) |
| **Actual Composition** | Multiple authors, c. 300 BCE – 100 BCE (possibly later for the Parables) |
| **Language** | Ge'ez (Ethiopic); Aramaic fragments at Qumran; some Greek fragments |
| **Audience** | Jewish scribal and priestly circles; later, Ethiopian Christians |
| **Genre** | Apocalyptic literature — heavenly journeys, angelic revelation, symbolic visions, testamentary wisdom |
| **Length** | 108 chapters across 5 originally separate books |
| **In One Sentence** | A visionary patriarch ascends to heaven, learns the secrets of cosmic order and divine judgment, and warns that the source of evil is angelic rebellion — but God will set everything right. |

---

## The Five Books of 1 Enoch

1 Enoch is not a single book but an anthology — five originally independent works collected under Enoch's name. Understanding this structure is essential for reading it well.

### 1. Book of the Watchers (Chapters 1–36)
**Date:** c. 300–200 BCE (among the oldest sections)
**Content:** The fall of the Watchers (angels who descended to mate with human women), the birth of the Nephilim (giants), the corruption of the earth, God's judgment through the archangels, and Enoch's cosmic journeys to the edges of creation — the chambers of the dead, the prison of fallen stars, the fragrant tree reserved for the righteous, and the accursed valley of Gehenna.
**Key themes:** The origin of evil in angelic rebellion (not human choice); the structure of the unseen world; divine judgment as cosmic restoration.
**Why it matters:** This section profoundly influenced how Second Temple Jews understood evil, demons, and the afterlife. The NT letter of Jude directly quotes 1 Enoch 1:9.

### 2. Book of Parables / Similitudes (Chapters 37–71)
**Date:** Debated — possibly 1st century BCE or 1st century CE. Notably absent from Qumran.
**Content:** Three "parables" (extended visions) centered on the **Son of Man** — a pre-existent, righteous figure who sits on God's throne and judges the kings and mighty ones. Also features the **Head of Days** (= Daniel's "Ancient of Days"), the **Lord of Spirits** (a distinctive Enochic title for God), and the final vindication of the righteous.
**Key themes:** Messianic expectation; the Son of Man as divine judge; the reversal of earthly power structures; the fate of the righteous dead.
**Why it matters:** The "Son of Man" language here is the closest pre-Christian Jewish parallel to how Jesus used the title in the Gospels. Whether Jesus knew this text, and whether its christology influenced early Christianity, are among the most debated questions in biblical studies.

### 3. Astronomical Book / Book of Luminaries (Chapters 72–82)
**Date:** c. 300–200 BCE (possibly the oldest section of 1 Enoch)
**Content:** Detailed astronomical instruction delivered by the angel Uriel — the movements of the sun through twelve gates, the phases of the moon, the winds, the four seasons, and the proper 364-day solar calendar.
**Key themes:** Cosmic order as divine law; the 364-day calendar (vs. the 354-day lunar calendar used in the Jerusalem temple); calendar controversy as theological dispute.
**Why it matters:** The calendar issue was explosive in Second Temple Judaism. The Qumran community (Dead Sea Scrolls) followed a solar calendar aligned with this book, putting them in direct conflict with the temple establishment. When 1 Enoch insists on a 364-day year, it is making a claim about who correctly follows God's cosmic order.

### 4. Book of Dreams (Chapters 83–90)
**Date:** c. 165–160 BCE (during the Maccabean crisis)
**Content:** Two dream-visions. The first is a brief vision of the flood. The second — the **Animal Apocalypse** — is an elaborate symbolic retelling of all Israelite history from Adam to the messianic age, in which humans are represented as animals: Adam is a white bull, Israel's patriarchs are bulls, the Israelites become sheep, their oppressors are wild beasts and birds of prey, and the Messiah appears at the end as a great white bull with huge horns.
**Key themes:** History as divinely scripted; Israel's suffering under angelic and human oppressors; the Maccabean revolt as the turning point before the end; messianic hope.
**Why it matters:** The Animal Apocalypse is one of the earliest datable apocalyptic texts and provides a window into how Jews during the Maccabean crisis understood their place in cosmic history.

### 5. Epistle of Enoch (Chapters 91–108)
**Date:** c. 200–100 BCE
**Content:** Enoch's testamentary exhortation to his children. Includes the famous **Apocalypse of Weeks** (93:1–10, 91:11–17) — a schematic division of all history into ten "weeks," from creation to the final judgment. Also contains a series of woes against the wealthy, the oppressors, and those who alter the truth.
**Key themes:** Theodicy (why the righteous suffer); the certainty of final judgment; the heavenly tablets as God's record of all deeds; hope for the righteous dead.
**Why it matters:** The Apocalypse of Weeks influenced later Jewish and Christian periodizations of history. The woe oracles anticipate the style of prophetic denunciation found in the Gospels.

---

## The World Behind the Text

1 Enoch emerged from the creative ferment of Second Temple Judaism (c. 515 BCE – 70 CE), a period when Jews were living under successive foreign empires — Persian, Greek, Ptolemaic, Seleucid, and eventually Roman. The traditional covenant framework ("obey God and prosper") was under strain: the righteous suffered while the wicked thrived, the temple priesthood was politically compromised, and the calendar itself was disputed.

Into this crisis, apocalyptic literature offered a new lens: the real story is happening in heaven. Evil has cosmic roots (angelic rebellion, not just human sin). God has a plan that encompasses all of history, and it is written on heavenly tablets. The righteous will be vindicated — if not in this life, then at the final judgment.

The **Ge'ez (Ethiopic)** text is the only complete version of 1 Enoch. The Ethiopian Orthodox Church, which has preserved this text as canonical scripture for over 1,500 years, deserves recognition as the guardian of a tradition that would otherwise have been lost. Aramaic fragments of all sections except the Book of Parables were found among the Dead Sea Scrolls at Qumran, confirming that 1 Enoch circulated widely in pre-Christian Judaism. Greek fragments survive in various manuscripts and quotations.

---

## Why This Book Was Written

Each section has its own immediate occasion, but the anthology as a whole addresses a persistent question: **Why is the world broken, and what is God doing about it?**

- The **Book of the Watchers** answers: evil entered the world through angelic transgression, not merely human failure. God will judge the angels and restore creation.
- The **Astronomical Book** answers: God's cosmic order is precise and knowable. Those who follow the wrong calendar are out of step with creation itself.
- The **Book of Dreams** answers: all of history — including Israel's current suffering — is part of God's plan, moving toward messianic restoration.
- The **Parables** answer: a pre-existent Son of Man will execute final judgment, overthrowing the powerful and vindicating the righteous.
- The **Epistle** answers: hold fast to righteousness. The wicked will be repaid. The heavenly tablets record everything.

---

## How to Read This Book

**Expect genre shifts.** You are reading five different books stitched together. The vivid narrative of chapters 1–36 gives way to the repetitive messianic visions of 37–71, then to the technical astronomy of 72–82, then to symbolic animal allegory in 83–90, and finally to testamentary exhortation in 91–108. Each section has its own voice and pace.

**Read the Watchers story (ch. 6–16) closely.** This is the foundational myth that drives the entire collection. The descent of 200 angels, led by Shemihazah, to Mount Hermon; their oath; their mating with human women; the birth of the giants; the teaching of forbidden knowledge by Azazel — this narrative provides the origin story for evil, violence, and corrupted knowledge that the rest of the book presupposes.

**Pay attention to the "Son of Man" in the Parables (ch. 37–71).** Whether you read this figure as a heavenly messiah, an angel, or a symbolic representation of the righteous community, the language is remarkable — and the overlap with Daniel 7 and the Gospels is unmistakable.

**Don't skip the Astronomical Book (ch. 72–82)** even though it reads like a technical manual. The ancient reader would have understood this as revelation about how God runs the universe. Calendar was not a trivial matter — it determined when to celebrate the festivals, and getting it wrong meant being out of sync with heaven.

**The Animal Apocalypse (ch. 85–90) requires a key.** White bulls = patriarchs. Sheep = Israel. Wolves, lions, eagles, etc. = foreign oppressors. Shepherds = angels appointed to govern Israel's punishment. The "great horn" that grows on one of the sheep (90:9) = Judas Maccabeus.

---

## The Threads — How This Book Connects

### Within 1 Enoch
- **Watchers → Giants → Evil Spirits → Final Judgment** — this causal chain runs from ch. 6 through ch. 16 and into the Parables and Epistle.
- **The 364-day calendar** in the Astronomical Book underlies the Apocalypse of Weeks' periodization of history.
- **Enoch's heavenly ascent** (ch. 14) is echoed in his final translation (ch. 70–71), forming a literary frame.

### With the Hebrew Bible / Old Testament
- **Genesis 5:24** ("Enoch walked with God, and he was not, for God took him") is the seed from which the entire Enoch tradition grows.
- **Genesis 6:1–4** (the "sons of God" who took "daughters of men") is expanded into the Watchers myth.
- **Daniel 7** (the "Ancient of Days" and "one like a son of man") is the direct source for the Parables' "Head of Days" and "Son of Man."
- **Isaiah 65:17** ("new heavens and new earth") parallels the "new creation" in 1 Enoch 72:1.

### With the New Testament
- **Jude 14–15** directly quotes 1 Enoch 1:9 — one of the only explicit quotations of a non-canonical text in the NT.
- **Jude 6** and **2 Peter 2:4** allude to the imprisoned angels of 1 Enoch 10–16.
- **Jesus' "Son of Man" sayings** in the Gospels resonate deeply with the Parables, though the direction of influence is debated.
- **Revelation's** imagery of cosmic judgment, the lake of fire, and the new creation echoes Enochic themes throughout.

### With the Dead Sea Scrolls
- Aramaic fragments of 1 Enoch (4QEn^a–g) confirm its popularity at Qumran.
- The **Book of Giants** (found at Qumran) is a spin-off of the Watchers narrative.
- The 364-day calendar in 1 Enoch aligns with the calendar used by the Qumran community.

---

## What a Modern Reader Might Miss

1. **The angel names mean something.** Shemihazah = "my name has seen" (possibly: "he sees the name [of God]"). Azazel = "God strengthens" or "scapegoat" (cf. Leviticus 16). Kokabi'el = "star of God." These are not random labels — they encode the angels' original dignities, making their fall more tragic.

2. **The "Watchers" are a class of angel.** The term comes from Daniel 4:13 (Aramaic *'ir*, "watcher"). In Enochic tradition, they were the highest-ranking angels assigned to watch over humanity — making their rebellion a betrayal of their cosmic mandate.

3. **1 Enoch's theology of evil is different from Genesis.** In Genesis 3, the origin of human sin is human choice (eating the fruit). In 1 Enoch, the origin of evil is angelic transgression — the Watchers introduced violence, weapons, sorcery, and corrupted knowledge. These two origin-of-evil traditions coexisted in Second Temple Judaism and were never fully reconciled.

4. **"Ten thousand times ten thousand" (1:9, 14:22) is a stock number for an innumerable heavenly host** — not a precise count. The same idiom appears in Daniel 7:10.

5. **The "fragrant tree" (ch. 24–25) is the tree of life.** It currently grows on one of the seven sacred mountains and will be given to the righteous after the final judgment. Its fragrance surpasses everything — a sensory image for paradise.

6. **The Ge'ez text is a translation of a translation.** The original was Aramaic (confirmed by Qumran fragments). It was translated into Greek, and then from Greek into Ge'ez. Each translation layer introduces potential distortion, which is why the Aramaic fragments (where they exist) are so valuable for reconstruction.

---

## Why This Book Isn't in Your Bible

1 Enoch is **canonical** in the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church and the Eritrean Orthodox Church — for them, it *is* in their Bible, and has been since at least the 4th century CE.

For most other Christian traditions, 1 Enoch was known and respected in the early centuries (quoted by Jude, cited by early church fathers like Tertullian, Irenaeus, and Clement of Alexandria) but was gradually excluded from the canon as the Western church consolidated its scriptures in the 4th–5th centuries. Reasons included:
- **Pseudepigraphy** — the recognition that Enoch did not actually write it
- **Theological concerns** — the Watchers myth and the Angel-Son of Man christology did not align easily with emerging orthodox theology
- **Loss of the text** — outside Ethiopia, the full Greek text was lost; the West knew only fragments and quotations

The book was effectively lost to Western scholarship until the Scottish explorer James Bruce brought three Ge'ez manuscripts from Ethiopia to Europe in 1773. The first English translation appeared in 1821. The Qumran discoveries (1947–1956) confirmed its antiquity and importance.

The scholarly consensus today is that 1 Enoch is indispensable for understanding Second Temple Judaism and the world in which Christianity emerged — regardless of one's view on its canonical status.

---

## Timeline

| Date (approx.) | Event |
|---|---|
| c. 300–200 BCE | Composition of the Astronomical Book (oldest section) and Book of the Watchers |
| c. 200–160 BCE | Composition of the Epistle of Enoch and the Apocalypse of Weeks |
| c. 165–160 BCE | Composition of the Animal Apocalypse (during Maccabean crisis) |
| c. 100 BCE – 1st c. CE | Composition of the Book of Parables (date debated; absent from Qumran) |
| c. 200 BCE – 68 CE | Aramaic copies circulate at Qumran (4QEn fragments) |
| c. 1st–2nd c. CE | Greek translation circulates; quoted by Jude 14–15 |
| c. 2nd–3rd c. CE | Cited favorably by Tertullian, Irenaeus, Clement of Alexandria |
| c. 4th c. CE | Translated into Ge'ez; becomes canonical in Ethiopian tradition |
| c. 4th–5th c. CE | Excluded from Western canons (Jerome, Augustine express reservations) |
| 1773 CE | James Bruce brings Ge'ez manuscripts to Europe |
| 1821 CE | First English translation by Richard Laurence |
| 1947–1956 CE | Aramaic fragments discovered at Qumran (Dead Sea Scrolls) |
| 1976 CE | Publication of *1 Enoch* in the Hermeneia commentary series (George W.E. Nickelsburg) |

---

*HESED notes: This guide was written for readers encountering 1 Enoch for the first time. It aims to provide historical context, literary orientation, and theological significance without editorializing on canonical questions. The Ethiopian Orthodox tradition's preservation of this text is a gift to all readers of ancient literature.*
